headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection/data-flow exposure from shared project-directory workflows; no direct compliance or critical harm pathway is evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A writes files in a shared project directory and has no self-isolation by default; Agent B has no file access or tool surfaces, so direct hijack is limited. Still, A’s file outputs can become attacker-controlled content if B is later wired to read them, and the shared directory is the only plausible bridge. Uncertainty about B’s runtime pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Agent B is configured to ingest files from the project directory, prompt-injection risk becomes active.
IF the shared project directory is used as an instruction channel, A can seed malicious content.
mitigations: Disable any file-based handoff from A to B.
Keep B read-isolated from the project directory.
Require explicit human review of A-generated files before reuse.
Use separate workspaces per agent.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent file transfers.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A can read and write the project directory and may touch generated source code, but B has no filesystem read, no network egress, and no declared data classes. That makes leakage from A to B unlikely unless an external orchestrator copies files into B’s context. The pair does not show a default sensitive-data path.
conditions: IF an orchestrator copies project files into B’s prompt, A’s file contents can leak into B’s context.
IF sensitive data is stored in the shared project directory, A can access it but B still lacks a direct read path.
mitigations: Do not place secrets in the project directory.
Keep B disconnected from file ingestion.
Use separate credentials and workspaces.
Review A outputs before any manual transfer to B.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has filesystem write and shell execution, while B has no write, shell, or subprocess capability. There is no overlapping mutable resource in the profiles, and B cannot contend on git or files directly. The only plausible conflict is indirect via an external orchestrator, so severity stays low.
conditions: IF both agents are later granted write access to the same directory, file contention can occur.
IF an orchestrator gives B write privileges not shown in the profile, conflict risk increases.
mitigations: Keep B read-only.
Assign distinct directories per agent.
Avoid concurrent runs on the same workspace.
Use a lock file if shared writes are introduced.
requires-engineering: add workspace arbitration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces generated source code and can offer to run it, but B is a game-playing agent with no action-taking or file-reading surface. There is no documented path where B consumes A’s outputs as authoritative by default. Any cascade would require extra orchestration not present in the profiles, so the risk is limited.
conditions: IF B is wired to treat A-generated code or text as authoritative input, cascading error risk appears.
IF A’s outputs are manually copied into B’s workflow, B may inherit A’s mistakes.
mitigations: Insert human verification between agents.
Do not auto-feed A outputs into B.
Keep B’s workflow independent of A artifacts.
Require tests or checks before reuse of A outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: No compliance mismatch is evidenced: A touches generated source code and handles an API key, while B declares no data classes, no network egress, and no residency or retention constraints. The profiles do not show PHI, EU PII, or regulated data flowing between them, so no compliance breach pathway is established.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into A’s project directory, compliance review is required.
IF B is later given access to regulated data classes, this verdict no longer applies.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the workspace.
Document data-class handling before deployment.
Review retention settings for A’s project files.
Do not grant B access to regulated datasets.
